La tachycardie : une accélération anormale et soudaine des battements cardiaques.La bradycardie : un ralentissement excessif du cœur, souvent sous les 50 battements par minute.Les extrasystoles : des battements prématurés ou "sauts" de cœur, très fréquents mais parfois ressentis comme des ratés.Les pauses cardiaques : un arrêt temporaire de la conduction électrique pendant quelques secondes.La fibrillation auriculaire : un rythme totalement irrégulier et anarchique des oreillettes                                                                                                                                              Le décollement d'une électrode : la sueur ou les mouvements peuvent détacher un capteur, créant des "artefacts" (parasites) sur le tracé.Le débranchement d'un câble : une déconnexion accidentelle d'un fil relié au boîtier.La batterie faible : une coupure d'alimentation qui arrête prématurément l'enregistrement.

Barotrauma / Volutrauma: High airway pressures or excessive volumes rupture fragile lung tissue, causing air leaks or a collapsed lung (pneumothorax).                                  Circuit Disconnection: The breathing tube or gas supply line detaches, leading to sudden loss of delivered volume and severe low oxygen (hypoxia).                                         Tube Obstruction: Mucus plugs, kinking, or biting of the endotracheal tube block airflow.                                                                                                                                                Equipment Malfunction: Power failures, gas source failures, or silent alarm faults prevent proper machine function.

Le débit libre (Free-flow) : La seringue est mal clipsée. Le piston s'actionne sous l'effet de la gravité. Le produit se vide instantanément chez le patient.Le bolus post-occlusion : Une tubulure se coude. La pression monte. L'infirmière plie la tubulure pour la déboucher. La pression accumulée libère un volume massif de produit d'un coup.Le retard d'alarme : Le moteur tourne mais le piston ne touche pas la seringue (mauvais calibrage). Le patient ne reçoit rien pendant des heures sans que l'appareil ne sonne.Erreur d'unité : Programmation d'un débit en ml/h au lieu de µg/kg/min. Cela multiplie par dix ou cent la dose requise.

Programming and Dosing Errors: Entering the wrong drug concentration or incorrect dose limits into smart pumps, frequently resulting in a tenfold overdose or complete failure to deliver adequate medication.PCA by Proxy: A well-meaning family member, visitor, or unauthorized staff member pressing the hand-held dosing button while the patient is asleep or sedated.Unsecured Syringe/Gravity Flow: Mechanical failures or unlatched syringe pistons allowing free-flow medication delivery driven purely by gravity instead of controlled pumping.Under-infusion Malfunctions: Device stalls, blocked lines, or hardware failures preventing scheduled or requested bolus doses from reaching the patient.

Infusion Set Blockages: Kinked cannulas, bent tubing, or dried insulin occluding the catheter can abruptly stop insulin delivery, triggering rapid hyperglycemia.Unintentional Delivery: Mechanical or software glitches can occasionally cause a "runaway pump" effect, delivering an unrequested bolus of insulin that leads to acute hypoglycemia.Site Complications: Local skin infections, bleeding, or adhesive failures can cause inflammation or leakage where the cannula enters the skin.User and Design Errors: Confusing interface layouts, missed alarms, or improper priming can interrupt therapy

Radiation Overdose: Incorrect default protocol settings or overriding safety alerts can subject patients to prolonged X-ray exposure.Human/Operational Error: Technicians accidentally repeating scans or failing to adjust parameters for smaller patients or children.Mechanical or Equipment Failure: Rare structural failures, such as loose gantry components or parts detaching during operations.Patient Identification Errors: Performing the wrong scan or scanning the incorrect body part due to miscommunication.

Projectile (Missile) Effects: Ferromagnetic objects like oxygen tanks, tools, IV poles, or personal metal items are violently pulled into the scanner.Thermal Burns: Conductive loops formed by cables, monitoring leads, or patient skin contact can cause radiofrequency-induced burns.Implant Malfunctions: Cardiac pacemakers or neurostimulators can malfunction or shift if not switched to an MRI-safe mode.Protocol Breaches: Unauthorized room access due to lapses in multi-zone security screening.

Equipment Malfunctions: Hardware or software crashes mid-procedure, or fluoroscopy beams failing to shut off when expected.Human and Process Errors: Misreading patient referrals, failing to verify patient identification, or X-raying the wrong body part.Training Gaps: Incorrect default settings or language barriers in equipment manuals leading to unintentional radiation overdoses.IT and Data Failures: Communication breakdowns in picture archiving and communication systems (PACS) or missing electronic orders
Normal Incidence: The sound beam hits the tissue boundary straight on at a 90-degree right angle.Oblique Incidence: The sound beam hits the tissue boundary at any angle that is not 90 degrees.

Equipment & Image Quality Deficiencies: Failing standard quality control tests, resulting in blurred, low-resolution, or unreadable images that could lead to missed diagnoses.Implant-Related Incidents: Rare physical complications during the mechanical compression phase of the exam, such as a breast implant rupture or leak.Personnel Non-Compliance: A radiology clinic operating without proper certification or utilizing an interpreting physician who does not meet the strict training standards required to read mammograms independently.                                         Craniocaudal (CC) Incident: A superior-to-inferior (top-to-bottom) view.Mediolateral Oblique (MLO) Incident: A lateral-to-medial view taken at an angle, which is essential for capturing the armpit area and the pectoral muscle.                        Interval Cancer Incidence: Cancers that appear symptomatically in the timeframe between two routine screening appointments after a previous "normal" reading.Screen-Detected Incidence: The overall rate of true positive breast cancer cases captured directly by annual or biennial mammograms.

Ventilator failure: Sudden mechanical stoppage, display errors, or internal leaks.Gas delivery issues: Pipeline disconnects, depleted gas cylinders, or vaporizer leaks.Circuit fires: Ignition from electrical devices or warmers interacting with high oxygen concentrations.Component blockages: Stuck unidirectional valves or exhausted/caked carbon dioxide absorbents.

Accidental Remote Activation: Research notes that anesthesiologists can unintentionally activate the table's remote control with their hips or thighs, causing the table to tilt mid-surgery.Table Tipping: Unlocking the floor wheels shifts the weight fulcrum. If a bariatric (obese) patient is repositioned without proper support staff, the entire table can tip over.Patient Falls: Medical malpractice cases often involve patients slipping off the table because straps were not secured before the table was tilted laterally to access organs like the appendix.Battery and Power Failures: Neglecting to charge the internal lead-acid battery can cause the table to lose power and freeze in a specific position during a procedure.

Structural Collapse: Ceiling suspension arms or heavy light heads fall mid-operation due to worn out components, vibrations, or broken securing screws.Thermal Burns: High-intensity LED or halogen convergence creates excessive radiant energy, leading to patient skin burns.Mechanical Drift: Suspension boom arms drift or drop unexpectedly during procedures, obstructing the sterile field.Airflow Disruption: Bulky lighthead shapes interfere with laminar airflow systems, potentially increasing infection risks

Patient Return Electrode Burns: Occurs when the dispersive grounding pad has poor adhesion, dries out, or is placed over scars, hair, or bony prominences, concentrating electrical current and causing thermal skin injuries.Stray Energy and Coupling: In monopolar or laparoscopic setups, capacitive coupling or direct insulation failure can transfer high-frequency electrical current to unintended internal tissues or organs.Operating Room Fires: Triggered when an ESU spark or active electrode ignites pooled alcohol-based skin preps or high concentrations of oxygen under surgical drapes.
